title: Post-Course Portfolio: E-commerce Backend
descriptionMarkdown:
# E-commerce Backend

## Position in the curriculum
Post-course portfolio expansion: build after finishing the full curriculum through the final capstone, and after the Authentication & User Management System, whose login/authorization component this project reuses directly for checkout. This is one of the harder catalog entries — treat it as a multi-week project, not a weekend one.

## Already-proven foundation
Every earlier catalog entry's individual skill (relationships, transactions, optimistic locking, authentication) converges here around one hard invariant: inventory must never go negative, even when two customers try to buy the last unit of the same product at the same instant.

## Project scope
Model `Product` (with a stock quantity), `Cart`, `Order` (with line items snapshotting price at time of purchase, never referencing the live product price), and `Payment` (simulated; no real payment gateway integration required, but design the interface as if a real one, like Stripe, would be swapped in later). A checkout endpoint must, in one transaction: verify and decrement stock for every line item (rejecting the whole order if any item is out of stock, using a real database constraint or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` to prevent a stock race, per Chapter 19), snapshot each line's price, and create the order. Make checkout idempotent against a retried request (an idempotency key on the checkout call, per Chapter 18) so a network retry cannot double-charge or double-decrement stock. Add order-status transitions (`PLACED` -> `SHIPPED` -> `DELIVERED`, or `CANCELLED`) as an explicit state machine, per Chapter 20's State pattern, not a bare string field checked by scattered conditionals.

## Required evidence
- A two-thread concurrency test buying the last unit of a product from two simultaneous checkout requests, confirming exactly one succeeds and the other receives a clear out-of-stock rejection, never a negative stock quantity.
- An idempotency test: retrying an identical checkout request (same idempotency key) after a simulated network failure produces exactly one order, not two.
- A test confirming an order's line-item prices remain fixed even after the underlying product's price later changes.
- A state-machine test confirming every valid and invalid order-status transition, including that a `DELIVERED` order cannot be cancelled.
- An authorization test confirming a customer can view only their own orders.

## Review and completion
A reviewer sets a product's stock to one unit, fires two simultaneous checkout requests for it from two different authenticated users, and expects exactly one order and one clear, well-formed rejection — never a race-condition negative stock count and never two successful orders for the same last unit.
learningObjectives: Prevent a stock-decrement race under real concurrent checkout with a database-enforced guarantee
Make a checkout endpoint idempotent against a retried request using an idempotency key
Snapshot transactional data (price at time of purchase) instead of referencing a mutable live value
Model order status as an explicit state machine with tested valid and invalid transitions
Combine authentication, transactions, and concurrency control in one coherent checkout flow
